en: The Sūtra on the High King of All Dharmas Spoken by the Buddha, also titled *The Sūtra on the King of the Meaning of All Dharmas*, translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
In the forest, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, who were formerly all brahmins with matted hair,
such as Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and others.

All were great Arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; their minds attained mastery, having well achieved liberation of mind and well achieved liberation by wisdom. They were great dragons among men, who had done what was to be done and accomplished their task; they had laid down the heavy burdens and attained their own benefit; they had exhausted all fetters of existence and well attained right knowledge; their minds were liberated from everything and they attained mastery, having reached the supreme shore.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month during the uposatha ceremony, the World-Honored One was seated in the open air, surrounded by and receiving the offerings and reverence of the assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, there was another bhikṣu who had recently left the household life and received the precepts on that very day; he went to where the World-Honored One was.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed the circumambulation, joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!”
I have newly left the household life and received the precepts this morning; I only pray that you will instruct me: how should I eat within the Saṃgha?
And having eaten within the Saṃgha, how may I digest it?
"Once food has been eaten, how is that gift digested?
Furthermore, son of good family, by faith in what meaning does one abandon the home life to go forth and obtain those benefits?
That other bhikṣu then questioned the Tathāgata in verse:
"I have only recently left the household life, having just received the precepts this morning;
I pray that you will explain for me: how should one consume the food of the Sangha?
For what purpose does one renounce the home?"
"Having left the household life to enter the Buddha-dharma, we only pray that you will explain the ultimate truth:
how should one consume the offerings given by others?
Having asked this, the Tathāgata replied to that bhikṣu:

“Bhikṣus, you should know that if a bhikṣu accomplishes three qualities, he should consume the food of the Saṅgha, and having consumed it, he shall digest the gift. For what purpose does that son of good family, out of faith, leave the home life for homelessness and obtain such benefit?”
What are these three?
Bhikṣus, you should know that they are:
entering the community of monks, performing the work of the community of monks, and being associated with the benefits of the community of monks.

"Monks, you should know that a monk who accomplishes these three qualities is worthy of consuming the food of the Saṅgha; having eaten it, he brings the gift to fruition. For what purpose does that son of good family, out of faith, leave the home life for homelessness and obtain such great benefit?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person enters among the Sangha And performs deeds worthy of the Sangha;
If they are in accord with the benefits of the Sangha, That person is able to digest offerings."
When this had been said, that bhikṣu spoke:
"The Blessed One has spoken this matter in brief; I am unable to understand it."
"Bhagavān!
How is it that a bhikṣu is said to have entered among the Saṃgha and performed the work of the Saṃgha?
Furthermore, how does he correspond to the benefits of the Saṃgha?"
Then that bhikṣu, immediately addressing the Tathāgata in verse, asked:
"How does one enter the Saṃgha?"
What is the activity of the Saṃgha?
What is the benefit of the Saṃgha?
We pray that you will explain this so that we may understand it.
Having been thus requested,
the Buddha said: "Bhikṣu!
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
I shall now explain to you extensively the Sangha, the deeds of the Sangha, and the benefits of the Sangha.
That bhikṣu said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“Monks! That which is called the Saṅgha consists of those who practice the four paths,
those who have attained the four fruits, and the eight types of individuals (pudgala).”

“Bhikṣus, you should know that this is called the Saṅgha; it is worthy of receiving offerings from the devas and humans of the world, and should be honored with palms joined; it is the unsurpassed field of merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“There are four practices and four attainments, And eight kinds of *pudgalas* (persons);”
"These are called the Saṅgha, the unsurpassed and supreme field of merit.
Having spoken thus,
that bhikṣu said:
“I do not know, World-Honored One!
What is the work of the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
“Monks! They are:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.”
“Monks, you should know that this is called the work of the Saṅgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“If one constantly and diligently cultivates The peaceful Eightfold Noble Path;”
"Practicing the supreme path in this way is what is called the work of the Saṅgha.
Having spoken thus, that bhikṣu said:
“I do not know, World-Honored One!
What is the benefit of the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
“Bhikkhus! What is called the benefit of the Saṅgha refers to the four fruits of the ascetic life. What are the four?
The four are as follows:
the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
Monks, you should know that these are called the benefits of the Saṅgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Great Man possesses great benefit; Such a person among the Saṃgha— Namely, one who has attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya— Is one who can truly consume offerings."
When this had been said, that bhikṣu replied:

"As the Blessed One has taught, a bhikṣu who enters the Saṃgha, performs the duties of the Saṃgha, and is worthy of the benefits of the Saṃgha—such a bhikṣu is able to digest the food of others; having eaten the food, he is able to digest the gifts of others."
"O Blessed One! For what reason does that son of good family leave the home life to go forth into homelessness and thereby obtain such benefit? "Son of good family!
[the Blessed One replied.]
If a person, aspiring for the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), leaves home to go forth into homelessness, I do not yet know, Blessed One:
does that person enter the Saṃgha?
Does he perform the deeds of a monk?
"Did you receive the benefit of the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
Excellent, excellent! You have reflected well;

you are well able to question; you possess excellent eloquence, being able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning as this. It benefits many people, brings happiness to many people, and provides welfare to many people. Out of compassion for the world, for its benefit, happiness, and peace, and out of compassion for devas and humans, you have asked thus.
As you have asked:

"If a person, aspiring for the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), leaves home to go forth into homelessness, does that *pudgala* enter the Saṃgha, perform the duties of the Saṃgha, and obtain the benefits of the Saṃgha?"
"To those who ask thus, I shall speak for you.
Bhikṣus, you should know that such a person does not enter the Saṃgha, nor does he perform the work of the Saṃgha; he is not in accord with the benefits of the Saṃgha."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“If a person aspires to bodhi, They do not enter among the Saṃgha;
They do not cultivate the deeds of the Saṃgha, Nor are they associated with the benefits of the Saṃgha.”
When this had been said, that bhikṣu spoke:
“I do not know, World-Honored One!

If that person has not entered the Saṃgha, does not perform the work of the Saṃgha, and is not associated with the benefits [of the Saṃgha], how is it that the World-Honored One permits his going forth and permits him to eat the food of the Saṃgha? How can he digest such offerings?”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! Cease, cease! Do not speak such words; this need not be asked."
Another bhikṣu spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
If this bhikṣu does not enter among the Saṃgha, does not perform the work of the Saṃgha, and is not associated with the benefits [of the Saṃgha], how can he digest the offerings?”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again:
"Bhikṣu! There is no need to ask this."
Another bhikṣu asked a third time:
"World-Honored One,
if this bhikṣu does not enter among the Saṃgha, does not perform the work of the Saṃgha, and does not correspond to the benefits [of the Saṃgha], how can he digest the offerings?"

At that time, because the bhikṣu had asked three times with such earnestness, the World-Honored One immediately emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated this trichiliocosm until its radiance filled it entirely; mountains, rivers, and rocky walls all vanished, and only the light was seen pervading this entire trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, the sentient beings within the ocean of this trichiliocosm—
namely, various fish, makaras, śuṃbhas, tortoises, and other such creatures— who had never before seen such a thing, were all struck with terror upon beholding the radiance.
Furthermore, among the great oceans of this trichiliocosm, the nāgas and nāga maidens, the asuras and asura maidens,
and the garuḍas and garuḍa maidens— who had never before seen such a thing— were all struck with awe and fear upon beholding the radiance.

In this way, that radiance reached everywhere throughout the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika-parṣadya, Mahābrahmā, Ābhāsvara, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara-śuddhāvāsa, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Akaniṣṭha, and even up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.

Thousands of devaputras, beholding the Buddha’s radiance, all came forth; from the trichiliocosm up to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and in succession even to the hosts of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, they all approached the place where the Buddha was with single-minded devotion. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet in respectful homage, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, they remained suspended in mid-air.

At that time, there were also many bhikṣus traveling among the people who, upon seeing the radiance, went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and sat down to one side with single-minded, correct mindfulness.

At that time, there were also bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who, having beheld the radiance, went to where the Buddha was. Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and sat down to one side with focused minds and right mindfulness.

At that time, there were also the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans from the three thousand great thousandfold world systems who, beholding the Buddha’s radiance, went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and sat down to one side with single-minded, correct mindfulness.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!
“World-Honored One! Many bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās have all gathered here.

Furthermore, many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and the Brahmakāyika heavens, up to thousands of sons of gods with purified bodies from the Immeasurable Purity realm—all have come to this assembly upon beholding the Buddha’s radiance.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you emit light from between your eyebrows? We pray that you will explain this for us.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Tathāgata in verse:
“Many thousands of sentient beings, And further, billions of nayutas;
Because they behold the Buddha’s radiance, They all come to see the World-Honored One!
For what reason, World-Honored One, [do they do so]?”
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions have these many billions of beings now gathered at this place?
World-Honored One, you know their meaning; for what reason have they come here?
“May the Guide, out of compassion, explain its cause to me.
Having asked this, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!...”
A newly ordained bhikṣu who had received the precepts that morning asked:

"If there is a bhikṣu who practices the Mahāyāna path and single-mindedly aspires for the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), how can such a person consume the food of the Saṃgha and be able to digest the offerings given by others?"
"Śāriputra! I now wish to answer the question of that bhikṣu.
For this purpose, immeasurable billions of sentient beings have gathered here."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One [will do so];
I pray only that the Sugata [will do so]!"
"Now I shall answer this question.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!
If this meaning were explained, some people would become confused and lost.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
All the great nāgas are inconceivable;
their possession of great supernormal powers and their great lion’s roar are inconceivable;
the lion’s roar itself is inconceivable.
The Dharma of the Great Beings is inconceivable.

This is not something that can be believed or understood by any ignorant ordinary beings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas; therefore, to your three questions, I remained silent and did not answer this matter.
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

In this assembly there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who are able to believe in this meaning. We only pray that the World-Honored One [will explain it].”
"Benefiting that person, he will answer my question.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"
"If this meaning were explained, sentient beings would become bewildered and submerged.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again addressed the Tathāgata in verse, saying:
"Excellent! We pray that you will now explain: What are the merits of a bodhisattva?"
"If one practices the bodhicitta, having heard this, one should exert diligent effort.
Having thus requested,
the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
“Śāriputra! The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world of devas, humans, and asuras. Śāriputra!
It is not that the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not digest the offerings made to him.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ultimately exhaust all giving.
Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva daily eats all the food and drink offered by sentient beings in morsels as large as Mount Sumeru, and wears a monastic robe as vast in measurement as Jambudvīpa, doing so constantly throughout kalpa after kalpa, such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva always remains thus, ultimately digesting the offerings.

“Śāriputra! Suppose a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were to provide daily seats for every single sentient being in the trichiliocosm, with each seat as vast and wide as the four continents and as high as Mount Sumeru, inlaid with the seven treasures.
What are the seven treasures? They are:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musāragalva, and agate; with these he adorned the lion throne, which was covered above with celestial garments.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were to receive such offerings from each and every sentient being day after day, and accept them for his own use as he pleases—whether for sitting, reclining, or other purposes.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva always receives in this manner and always uses in this manner, they ultimately consume the offerings. Why is this?

Śāriputra! From the very first moment a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves upon the mind of enlightenment, from that day forward, they become a field of merit for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and sentient beings.

“Śāriputra! For each and every sentient being, on day after day, there are palaces of such color with seven locations, their dimensions as vast and long as the four continents—namely, Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru—which are thus broad and long;
in each distinct location, curtains of the seven precious jewels hang down.

In each of those places, there were high banners, pennants, and canopies draped with nets of the seven treasures, adorned with various celestial jewels; those palaces were so vast and lofty as to reach the realm of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.
In each of those places, various jewel-trees were found everywhere;
from all those trees, whatever was desired by one's will could be obtained, and from every single tree issued forth the sound of music.
Among those trees, some are able to produce various kinds of fragrances, some are able to produce various exquisite flowers, and some are able to produce various fruits.
In that palace and in those places there are many ponds, filled with water possessing the eight qualities;
their bottoms are strewn with golden sand, and they are filled with lotuses made of the seven precious gems.
All those ponds have stairways made of lapis lazuli, and their perimeters are surrounded by railings of the seven precious gems.

Along the banks of those ponds, there are many countless lion thrones, upon which billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of cushions are spread, and celestial, exquisite flowers are scattered everywhere across the ground.
Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses such a colored palace, such a colored seat, and such a colored dwelling, whether sitting, lying down, walking, standing, speaking, or remaining silent, all shall accord with their will.
Śāriputra! If all sentient beings, day after day, were to obtain and enjoy such palaces, such seats, and such dwellings as these in color, Śāriputra!
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva ultimately consumes the offerings of all sentient beings, and so it is even for those who have only first resolved their minds [for enlightenment]. Why is this?
“Śāriputra! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings. Śāriputra!”
You now behold these noble lineages, great wealth, abundant riches, and supreme bliss—namely:

the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, the great clans of Śreṣṭhins, and the great clans of Gṛhapatis; kings among men, Cakravartin wheel-turning monarchs endowed with the seven treasures; the gods of the Four Great Kings, Śakra Devendra of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, Suyāma devaputra, Tuṣita devaputra, Nirmāṇarati devaputra, and likewise the Paranirmitavaśavartin devaputras; the Brahmā Sahāmpati, and so on in succession up to the beings born in the realms of the Form and Formless Heavens.

Śāriputra, if there are those who abide in the first fruit, the second fruit, the third fruit, or the fourth fruit; or those who have attained the path of a pratyekabuddha; or those who wish to awaken to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—[it is for them that this is taught].
All such things as these are born within Bodhisattvas and are transformed by Bodhisattvas; they should be understood in this way.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have practiced the bodhisattva path, they successively attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having awakened, they turn the wheel of Dharma; and when those who are bodhisattvas hear the Dharma from them, they thus enter the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, the fruit of *arhat*, and the path of the *pratyekabuddha*, proceeding in succession up to the awakening of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Having heard [the teaching on] giving, they are able to practice giving; by means of that giving, they are born into great clans of Kṣatriyas, great clans of Brāhmaṇas, or great clans of householders, and they become human kings or *cakravartin* universal monarchs.

Having heard the exposition of the precepts, one is able to receive and uphold them; by upholding the precepts, one is born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Heavens, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin.
Having heard of the four immeasurables, one practices them; through such practice, one is born in the heavens of the Form Realm.
Śāriputra! This gate should be well understood in this way: all these dharmas depend upon the bodhisattva and that which is transformed by the bodhisattva. Śāriputra!
For example, from the abode of Lake Anavatapta, the Dragon King’s pool, four great rivers emerge.
What are these four?
They are as follows:
The Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Vakṣu, and the Sītā—these are the great rivers.
These four great rivers flow into the four great oceans. What are the four?
The great river Gaṅgā flows with five hundred tributaries to fill the eastern sea;
the great river Sindhu flows with five hundred tributaries to fill the southern sea;
the great river Vakṣu flows with five hundred tributaries to fill the western sea.
The great river Sītā has five hundred tributaries flowing to fill the Northern Sea.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
These four great rivers flow toward the four directions, entering the four great oceans in their respective order.
Śāriputra, as those four great rivers flow toward the four directions, would there be any sentient beings who might have need of them?
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
“Immeasurable sentient beings receive and enjoy its power, namely:
śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.”
"World-Honored One!

Those four great rivers are all able to completely fill rice fields, bean fields, fields of masha beans, and fields of large and small wheat; they are able to pervade all various kinds of grains, beans, and the like."
"Those grains, beans, and so forth are enjoyed by many people, namely:
śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, non-humans, and others.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
Is there any sentient being who does not have need of those four great oceans?”
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Immeasurable sentient beings receive and enjoy the attainment of power, namely:
He excels over sentient beings of the land and sentient beings of the water, namely:
fish, tortoises, makaras, timiṅgilas, frogs, geese, ducks, and fishermen.
Furthermore, it is the dwelling place of immeasurable great beings, namely:
the nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and so forth.
Immeasurable beings, both human and non-human, derive benefit and power from its enjoyment, namely:
Jewels, pearls, and lapis lazuli; *ka-ya* and coral; great sapphire-blue *indranīla* gems; *musāragalva* gems, *karketana* gems, and agate gems, and so forth.
Furthermore, there is another precious great jewel of immense value that is used by people within the great ocean.
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
"What do you think? By what causes and conditions do those four great oceans possess such power?
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"Such is the power of the causal conditions of the waters of Lake Anavatapta, the Dragon King.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
Śāriputra! The Nāga King Anavatapta is free from three kinds of fear.
What are these three?
That is to say:
attaining freedom from the fear of garuḍas;
freedom from the fear of hot sands;
When other dragon kings engage in sexual desire, they assume the form and appearance of snakes; however, when that Dragon King Anavatapta engages in sexual desire, he does not take on such a form.
Śāriputra! There, within the palace of the nāga king Anavatapta, a bhikṣu who practices dhyāna resides. Śāriputra!
Within the palace of the Nāga King Anavatapta, there dwell bhikṣus of supernatural power and majestic virtue. Śāriputra,
in whichever palace the Nāga King Anavatapta resides, whoever enters it shall be free from all decline and affliction.
The venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare, World-Honored One!”
The palace of the Naga King Anavatapta has accomplished such unprecedented qualities.
How rare, World-Honored One!
Within such a naga palace, all three kinds of faults are entirely absent.
How rare, World-Honored One!
Whatever sentient beings enter that palace are spared from the three kinds of faults.
How rare, World-Honored One!
A bhikṣu who dwells in meditative concentration, possessing supernatural powers and majestic virtue, enters and resides in that palace of the nāga king.
How marvelous, World-Honored One!
From that nāga lake emerge four great rivers, which many people enjoy and utilize.

Those four great rivers give rise to the four great oceans, which are the dwelling places of the great multitudes of sentient beings and the locus where immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings enjoy their sustenance— namely,
the dwelling places enjoyed by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, humans and non-humans, and so forth.
“World-Honored One!
The Naga King Anavatapta has accomplished such immeasurable merits.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, it is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Śāriputra!”
For example, the Nāga King Anavatapta is free from three kinds of fear.
Śāriputra, in the same way,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva has likewise attained transcendence and is free from the fear of the three evil realms.
What are the three fears?
First, the fear of hell; second, the fear of hungry ghosts; third, the fear of animals. "Śāriputra!
For example, Śāriputra, just as the waters of the Lake of Anavatapta, the Dragon King, flow forth as four great rivers for the enjoyment of many people,
so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: they gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu).
What are the four?
They are generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
These four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are practiced by bodhisattvas and enjoyed by many people.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as it is because of the causal conditions of the lake of the Nāga King Anavatapta that there are the four great oceans, even so it is."
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva gives birth to the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
"Just as the great ocean provides a dwelling place of peace and happiness for immeasurable sentient beings,
even so, Śāriputra!"
Sentient beings within the three realms of existence attain peaceful dwelling by relying on omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
These three are: the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Śāriputra! This gateway is thus;
you should understand it well.
“Śāriputra! All the peace and happiness of sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm arise entirely because of bodhisattvas and exist in dependence upon bodhisattvas.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
those who have resolved upon bodhicitta practice it constantly and without interruption, continuing in succession until they receive their prediction of enlightenment.
Having received the prediction, they awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*);

having awakened to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they turn the wheel of Dharma—a wheel of such true Dharma that no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, Brahmās, or anyone else can ever turn.
Because they hear the Dharma, the fourfold assembly—namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—is produced;
through those causes and conditions, they attain immeasurable happiness, the happiness of gods and humans, and the happiness of liberation.
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
From what does this dharma arise?”
The venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
they are born from the Bodhisattva.”
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, what do you think?"

Included within the three realms of existence, whether it be profit or sustenance, whatever things there may be are all the result of the kindness previously bestowed by the Bodhisattva; how could there be anyone capable of repaying such kindness?
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One,
there is no one capable of repaying it.”
"Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva gives birth to all dharmas.
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! It is, for example, as if there were a person who was poor and possessed no wealth, while another great wealthy person possessed abundant riches; out of a heart of compassion, the latter would relinquish and bestow them upon the former—giving away many hundreds, many thousands, immeasurable, incalculable, and even hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.”

In this same sequence, one gives to a second person, a third person, and a fourth person, and so on until one hundred thousand, even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, and thus even unto all sentient beings.
That great wealthy person gives away all his possessions;
furthermore, he bestows fearlessness upon all, causing them to eliminate their terrors, and ensures they are liberated from all such fears as enmity, hatred, bondage, and strife;
moreover, he causes them to be free from the fear of the evil realms.
Furthermore, it brings peace and happiness to immeasurable devas and humans.

Among those who receive such gifts, there may be a single sentient being who, out of gratitude, divides one of their own possessions into a hundred parts and gives one part to the original donor. Having given the object, they form this thought:
"I have repaid my debt of gratitude."
"Śāriputra! What do you think?

If this man thus benefits all sentient beings and thus brings such advantage to all sentient beings, and if one were to give to the previous donor a single hundredth part of the object destroyed by that one sentient being, would that exhaust his debt of gratitude?"
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One,
it cannot be exhausted.”
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Śāriputra!
It is the same for the bodhisattva."

Śāriputra! Suppose there were one who benefits all beings through a heart of compassion, and another person who gives a hundredth part of a single being or a single object to that compassionate one. [The latter’s merit would be greater.]
"So it is, so it is, Śāriputra!

Suppose there is a donor who provides all manner of desired pleasures, offerings, and attendances to a practitioner of the Mahāyāna until the end of their life; even though that person makes such offerings, they still do not repay the debt of gratitude."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!”
"You are now truly my disciple!
You follow my teaching and skillfully understand my words,
Śāriputra!"

If all sentient beings were to give up their own flesh, or skin, or sinews, or bones, or even their entire bodies—doing so hundreds of thousands of times—they would not repay even one hundredth of the Bodhisattva’s kindness;
nor would they repay one-thousandth, ten-millionth, or even one-hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor any calculable fraction thereof, for it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
the kindness of a bodhisattva cannot be repaid by the gods, humans, asuras, and others in the world.
“Śāriputra! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives rise to the mind of omniscience of the Tathāgata, they will then be able to repay his kindness. Why is this?
“Śāriputra! If there are those who can resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they shall be the object of enjoyment for all sentient beings. Śāriputra!”
For example, suppose a sandalwood tree were to grow here in Jambudvīpa; when its sprouts first emerge, they are already able to eliminate diseases treatable by medicinal herbs for boys and girls;
when its leaves emerge, they can eliminate the diseases of women and men;
and as it further grows into a full-grown sandalwood tree, if anyone comes to dwell within its shade, that person is freed from illness.
When those sandalwood trees produce flowers, they can bestow celestial music;

when those sandalwood trees bear fruit, their radiance pervades the worlds of the ten directions, and whichever sentient beings recall them with mindfulness upon that light appearing shall attain the state of being neither subject to aging nor illness;
and if those sandalwood trees are cut down, split, or broken apart, and their timber is taken away, one need not fear poverty.
If there were someone who could take the timber of that sandalwood tree to construct a dwelling, anyone who entered it would experience neither cold nor heat, and neither hunger nor thirst.

"So it is, so it is! Śāriputra, that sandalwood tree is entirely useful; there is nothing about it that is not useful. From the moment the tree first sprouts, it is already fit for use; once grown, it is useful; as it increases, it is useful; when flowers appear, it is useful; when fruit appears, it is useful; when it is cut down, split, and made into timber, it is useful; and when used to build a house, it is useful."

“Śāriputra! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: when first resolving to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they cultivate the four saṃgraha-vastus to bestow happiness upon sentient beings, like the sprouts of sandalwood.
Once that resolve has been made, their mind increases in the three gates of liberation. What are these three?
That is to say:
the gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are like the growth of leaves on a tree;
subsequently, attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is like the growth of the tree itself.
Next, the accomplishment of the wisdom of all-knowledge is like the blossoming of flowers on a tree;
next, entering the realm of nirvana without remainder is like the presence of fruit on a tree.

The bodily relics, as small as mustard seeds, remain to sustain and benefit the realms of sentient beings, just as when people cut down a sandalwood tree and carry away the wood, the Tathāgata’s relics likewise benefit sentient beings in the same manner.

Just as when one takes wood from a sandalwood tree to build a house, those who enter it find peace and happiness, so too, after the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa, all practitioners who enter the temple of the Tathāgata are freed from heat and attain refreshing coolness.
Śāriputra! This gateway is thus; you should understand it well. Śāriputra!

If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddha-dharma will not be interrupted; all sentient beings will attain the happiness of gods and humans as well as the happiness of liberation, and they shall constantly practice without cessation.
“Śāriputra! If the bliss of gods and humans and the bliss of liberation were practiced constantly and without interruption, Śāriputra!
Could anyone possibly describe anything that is similar to or equal to them?”
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

No one can be equal to them; whether among those persons, devas, and humans, or including the Brahmās, asuras, and the world, even if they were to provide them with virtuous happiness, they could not repay their kindness—not in one kalpa, nor in a hundred kalpas, nor in a thousand kalpas, nor in ten million kalpas, nor even in ten billion kalpas.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, Śāriputra."
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to repay all unsurpassed debts of gratitude, that person should resolve their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Śāriputra! This generation of the mind is the unsurpassed repayment of gratitude; it is a repayment of gratitude that corresponds exactly to the kindness received. There is no sentient being who is its equal, and there is no sentient being by which it can be compared.
One who wishes to repay that kindness should give rise to a mind of non-attachment and give rise to this unsurpassed mind. "Śāriputra!
One who wishes to repay the kindness of the Tathāgatas of the past should only resolve to attain this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Śāriputra! Those who wish to repay the kindness of future Tathāgatas must likewise resolve to give rise to this mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Śāriputra!

If one wishes to repay the unsurpassed kindness of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who currently exist, currently live, and currently abide throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one must likewise resolve to attain this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Śāriputra! There are two kinds of persons whose offerings to the Tathāgata constitute unsurpassed offerings. What are these two?
"There are persons whose all outflows are exhausted; there are persons who give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I speak of two types of persons Who make offerings to the Tathāgata!"
The Bodhisattva and the Arhat—these two are *pudgalas*.
Not with worldly wealth, nor with the means of subsistence found within the three realms of existence, can one perform a true offering;
only by such [spiritual offerings] can one truly honor those Great Beings.
If one offers the most excellent forms, sounds, tastes,
and textures among gods and humans to that Great Being, it is not called a "good offering.
If it is an offering of material requisites, it is not the unsurpassed offering.
If one gives rise to the bodhicitta, this is the unsurpassed offering.
Whether among gods, humans, or the world of Māras,
even if all those who desire it were to grant [their wishes], this would not be the supreme way of repaying their kindness.
Great beings are never lacking; they do not give rise to a mind of longing.
For such great beings, there is no superior offering.
If a person’s mind harbors longing, they offer the unsurpassed worship to the Buddha.
Having resolved upon bodhicitta, they shall attain Buddhahood in the future.
If a person constantly aspires and desires to perform immeasurable merit,
they should resolve upon bodhicitta with firm and diligent vigor.
If a person desires and aspires, And resolves to cultivate the immeasurables;
That person exerts diligence, Desiring to attain the Buddha’s bodhi.
If a person aspires to celestial bliss And seeks to abandon all suffering;
That person then cultivates the causes and conditions for the Buddha’s bodhi.
If they wish to see immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya Buddhas;
with right faith and a sincere heart, desiring to attain the Buddha’s bodhi.
If a person wishes to travel to Immeasurable and diverse worlds;
That person must apply diligent effort Desiring to attain the Buddha’s Bodhi.
If one wishes to see past Buddhas, One should maintain such a recollection.
They have resolved their minds on enlightenment and practice the conduct of enlightenment.
If anyone wishes to behold the Buddhas of future ages,
they should resolve their minds on enlightenment and practice the conduct of enlightenment.
If one wishes to see and make offerings to the Buddhas of the present age,
that person’s mind will aspire to benefit all sentient beings.
If a person possesses universal compassion and pities all sentient beings;
If that person wishes to give rise to the unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi;
if they wish to bestow upon sentient beings unsurpassed and immeasurable bliss;
that person wishes to give rise to the foremost Buddha-bodhi.
If one sees suffering beings and gives rise to a heart of compassion,
that person desires to initiate the causes and conditions for the Buddha’s bodhi.
If such a mind is produced, thinking, "I shall awaken to the unsurpassed path," [then one is established in the stage of a bodhisattva].
"Those immeasurable merits cannot all be told.
Having spoken thus,
the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the Dharma that the World-Honored One has previously taught, how many sentient beings have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
“Śāriputra, stop, stop! Śāriputra!”
Why do you now ask about such a meaning?
For what reason? Śāriputra!
If the Tathāgata were to explain this meaning with his omniscient wisdom, sentient beings would become confused.
Why is that? Śāriputra!
Because the Buddha-Tathāgata possesses immeasurable precepts, immeasurable samādhis, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable supernormal powers, and immeasurable knowledge. Śāriputra!
"For example, space cannot be measured or grasped.
How is this so? Can space be conceived?
The Venerable Śāriputra replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is inconceivable. Why is this?
"Because that space has not been known by anyone in the past, is not being known now,
and will not be known in the future. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Śāriputra! That which the Tathāgata knows cannot be known by any sentient beings, any śrāvakas, or any pratyekabuddhas—whether they have already known it, know it now, or will know it in the future.
"Why is this? That which the Buddha knows is not within the realm of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare it is, World-Honored One!
That those sentient beings possess such a well-determined mind as to resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha said: "So it is,
so it is, Śāriputra!"
"There must be bodhisattvas whose minds are well-resolved.
The Venerable Śāriputra said,
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva become one whose mind is well-determined?
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!

Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa—whether they move on land, in water, through the air, or upon the earth—all such sentient beings, having exhausted their previous forms, were to obtain human bodies;
and suppose there were one person who taught those people and caused them to abide in the five precepts and the path of ten wholesome actions.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit?
Śāriputra said, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
"The merit of that person is beyond analogy.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"

I shall further explain this, which you should now know: if someone were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the five precepts and the path of the ten wholesome actions, and another person were to cause even a single sentient being to abide in the Dharma of faithful practice, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the dharma of faithful practice, would that person, by reason of this cause, obtain much merit?
Śāriputra said: "Very many,
World-Honored One!"
"The merit of that person cannot be described by even a small fraction of a simile.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"

If such a person causes all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the path of practice through faith, and if another person were to cause even a single sentient being to abide in the path of practice through the Dharma, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former.
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the Dharma and practice the Path, would that person, by reason of this, obtain much merit?”
Śāriputra said:
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"The merit of that person is beyond analogy.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"

If such a person causes all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the Dharma and practice the Path, the merit thereof is surpassed by that of another person who causes even a single sentient being to abide in the first fruit [of the path].
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the first fruit [of the path], would that person, by reason of this, obtain much merit?”
Śāriputra said:
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"The merit of that person is beyond comparison.
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra!..."

If such a person causes all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the first fruit, and if another person were to cause a single sentient being to abide in the second fruit, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former.
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the second fruit, would that person, by reason of this, obtain much merit?”
Śāriputra said, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
"The merit of that person is beyond comparison.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,

"If such a person causes all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the second fruit, and another person were to cause a single sentient being to abide in the third fruit, the latter's merit would surpass the former."

“Śāriputra! If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the third fruit, and another person who caused a single sentient being to abide in the fruit of arhatship, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former.

“Śāriputra! If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the fruit of arhatship, and if there were another person who caused a single sentient being to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former.

“Śāriputra! If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the path of a pratyekabuddha, and another person who caused even a single sentient being to abide in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former.”

“Śāriputra! If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and if there were another person who caused a single sentient being to abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former.”

“Śāriputra! If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to abide in the dharma of non-retrogression, and another person who caused a single sentient being to ultimately abide in the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former.”
“Śāriputra! If there were someone who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to ultimately abide in the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti),
and if there were another person who caused a single sentient being to swiftly abide in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former.”
“Śāriputra! Suppose there were a person who caused all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to swiftly and securely abide in the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*),

and suppose there were another person who extensively expounded for others this ‘Dharma-gate of the Supreme King’— this teaching of all dharmas which can generate bodhi, destroy Māra, demonstrate that the aggregates (*skandha*) are without self so that one may leave behind the realms (*dhātu*), disperse the sense-bases (*āyatana*), utterly extinguish afflictions, and destroy the defiled portion while purifying the seeds of the pure portion— the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former.”
“Śāriputra! Setting aside all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa. Śāriputra!”

For example, suppose all sentient beings throughout the four continents of a world system, and likewise throughout a thousand-world system, a two-thousand-world system, a three-thousand-world system, and even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of worlds—extending in this way through the ten directions of east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, and above and below—in each and every direction, there were sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; whether they possessed form or were formless, moved on land or in water, and whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation—even including those with perception and those without perception—if the bodies of all such sentient beings were exhausted and they all attained human birth, and if a single person were to instruct all those people and cause them to abide in the five precepts and the path of the ten wholesome actions.
“Śāriputra!
Would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, obtain much merit?
Śāriputra replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Sugata! They will obtain immeasurable, incalculable merit.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, you should now understand this parable. Śāriputra!

Śāriputra, suppose there were a person who established all sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions in the stage of faith-practice (*śraddhācaryā*), the stage of dharma-practice (*dharmacaryā*), the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), the path of the pratyekabuddha, the dwelling in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the state of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-dharma*), the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*);

and suppose there were another person who, for the sake of others, extensively expounded this "Dharma-Gate of the High King" (*Sarvadharmanirdeśa-uccakrājarāja-dharmaparyāya*). Śāriputra, [the latter would obtain] the merit resulting from this.
This accumulation of merit surpasses the previous merit; it is foremost, pure, unsurpassed, and incomparable. "Śāriputra!
This supreme Dharma-gate is that which is practiced by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of well-settled mind; such is the conduct of a bodhisattva, as it should be known."
Śāriputra! If anyone should hear this Dharma-door of the High King of All Dharmas, you should know that such a person is indeed a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
that person shall not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He is the field of merit; he is the unequaled; he is the peerless; he is the one worthy of mindfulness;
he is the one who brings across; he is the one who is tranquil; he is the tamer; he is by nature serene;
he is the liberated one; he is the great man; he is the lion; he is the foremost of men.
He is the Supreme Man, the Great Being, the Dragon, the Deva, the Deva among Devas,
the Unobstructed One, the Unbound One, the Doer of What Must Be Done, the One Who Has Accomplished His Task,
the One for Whom All That Was to Be Done Is Fully Accomplished; he is, indeed, the Mass of Boundless Merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person practices for enlightenment, They are a being of certain resolve;
That person has no evil intent, And within them dwells the Tathāgata of Ignorance."
If one gives rise to the bodhicitta, its merit is beyond comparison;
among all the merits in every world, none equal the merit of bodhicitta.
Within boundless worlds, for all sentient beings that exist—
If a person causes [others] to excel, And causes them to advance further and further,
That person, progressing higher and higher, Attains superior and superior merit and benefit;
Compared to the merit of this bodhicitta, Their own merit is like a mere speck of dust.
If a person extensively expounds this unsurpassed sūtra,
as well as those who study this scripture, such persons are fields of merit.
If a person hears this sūtra, their fundamental nature will be completely purified.
Such a person is named "Tranquil," a true son of the Buddha.
When hearing this sutra, he is a courageous and discerning man;
he is called a "Tamer" and "Liberated," a lion among the gods of gods.
"If one speaks this sutra, it is the unsurpassed sutra among all sutras;
the God of gods among gods, and the unsurpassed among all sentient beings.
Having spoken thus, [he continued].
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare, World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgata has been able to thus briefly explain the conduct of bodhisattvas within this sutra.
Yet, even though bodhisattvas practice the bodhisattva path for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), they still have not yet attained the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
This sutra speaks of the unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom. World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate from the mouth of the Tathāgata, such sentient beings will swiftly obtain excellent benefit—the foremost excellent benefit.”
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, even those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who have already entered parinirvāṇa in the past, have already preached this Dharma-gate for the sake of sentient beings; of all the Dharmas taught by those past Buddhas, this Dharma-gate is the most supreme.”

"Bhagavān! In future ages, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, shall preach this Dharma-gate for the sake of sentient beings. Among all the teachings spoken by those future Buddhas, this Dharma-gate is the most supreme; it is called the 'Dharma-gate of the High King of All Dharmas.'"
"Bhagavān!

At this present time, those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who currently live, exist, and abide, are now teaching this Dharma-gate for the sake of sentient beings; among all the teachings spoken by those present Buddhas, this Dharma-gate is the foremost."
"Bhagavān! I have already heard many Dharma-gates from the Bhagavān in the past. Excellent, Bhagavān!
May you now further expound this Dharma-gate for me."
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!
As for this sūtra, the Buddha himself knows the proper time; he speaks according to his knowledge of the minds of sentient beings, in accordance with their inclinations and understandings.”
"Śāriputra! This is what the Buddha knows; it is not within the realm of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Śāriputra! [he continued.]

When this Dharma was being taught, eighty-four thousand people who had never before resolved their minds toward Bodhi now heard this sutra and resolved their minds toward Bodhi; sixty thousand sentient beings attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

There were seven billion devas of the desire realm who had never before resolved their minds toward Bodhi, and upon hearing this sutra, they resolved their minds toward Bodhi; three hundred million sentient beings attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
Immeasurable earth-dwelling devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, who had never before resolved their minds toward Bodhi, now heard this sutra and resolved their minds toward Bodhi.
“Śāriputra! Because the Tathāgata perceives and understands this meaning, he extensively expounds this Dharma-gate for the sake of sentient beings.

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—joined their palms toward the Buddha, gazing up at his venerable countenance without averting their eyes for even a moment.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled serenely, emitting immeasurable colors from his face. Various colored rays of light shone everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm; once this supreme radiance had pervaded all, it returned and entered the World-Honored One’s face.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what cause and for what reason does the World-Honored One smile in this way?”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!
Do you see these many bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, who stand with palms joined, gazing at the Buddha without for a moment averting their eyes?
Śāriputra said:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra! These fourfold assemblies practice the Mahāyāna path and perform the bodhisattva deeds.”
Śāriputra! Such mental activities as those, I know them all. Śāriputra!
If the Tathāgata was not obtained in the past, will not be obtained in the future, and is not obtained in the present— Śāriputra!
this course of action of sentient beings is not obtained within the aggregates (skandha), not obtained within the elements (dhātu), and not grasped within the sense-bases (āyatana).
"Śāriputra! This bodhisattva practice is unsurpassed and peerless.
When the Tathāgata spoke these words concerning the bodhisattva practice, this trichiliocosm shook violently throughout its entirety, namely:
It shook, shook everywhere, and shook equally everywhere;
it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere;
it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere.
Arising, arising everywhere, and arising equally everywhere;
awakening, awakening everywhere, and awakening equally everywhere.
Māra the Evil One retreated from his palace, and all other demonic beings likewise fell away.
Regarding this, there is a verse that says:
"The power of Māra’s army was destroyed this morning; It cannot rise up again.
By what has been taught by the Perfectly Awakened One, Everything is entirely without remainder."
The māras of the aggregates and the māras of afflictions are emaciated and lack power,
for they have heard the Tathāgata teach that all phenomena are empty.
Seeing all these māras struck with terror, they hear the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
"Since those phenomena do not arise, how could there be death?
After Māra Pāpīyas had fallen to the ground, he addressed the Tathāgata in verse:
"Excellent, O Great Solitary Buddha!"
"May you quickly comfort me;
I now fear my life will end, bound as I am by grief and anxiety.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas, having received the Buddha’s consolation, suddenly vanished.

When the Tathāgata had finished teaching this Dharma-gate, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced in his heart; and those newly ordained bhikṣus who had not yet completed their summer retreats, along with the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, all rejoiced greatly upon hearing what the World-Honored One had spoken.
The Record of the Translation of the *Sarvadharmābhyudgatarāja-sūtra*, also known in the Dan edition as the *Sarvadharmārtharāja-sūtra*.

Now, when imperial virtue accords with Heaven, the minister responds to the Sage Way. The Great Chancellor of Wei, the King of Bohai, mysteriously encountered the titles of the Tathāgata’s supreme scriptures, namely the *Sarvadharmābhyudgatarāja-sūtra*.

The Prince, High Duke Yi Tong, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was one who understood the Dharma. Relying on the merit of his supreme translations and his preeminence in understanding the Dharma, he respectfully compiled the Sanskrit texts and redoubled his devotion to this work. Moved by the power of the Buddha-Dharma and having encountered this sublime scripture, he commissioned those who knew the Dharma to translate it into the Wei language.
Translated at Dingchang Monastery by the Mahāyāna student śramaṇa Tánlín and the visiting Brahmin Gautama Liuzhī, under the patronage of General Dòu.

On the twenty-third day of the sixth month of the late summer in the fourth year of the Xìnghé era, the cyclical year being Rénxū, the day being Dǐwèi followed by Dīngsì, this work consisting of eight thousand four hundred and forty-nine characters was first translated.

The merit of producing this sutra is beyond the measure of ordinary knowledge; were it to have a physical form, even the realm of empty space could not contain it. For those who transcribe, recite, and make offerings to it, they shall dwell but briefly in the cycle of birth and death, and Bodhi will not be far off.
Any wise man or woman who sees, hears, or knows this, should aspire to honor and cultivate this merit.
